name: Ceph
vendor: Ceph Foundation (Linux Foundation); IBM is the premier sponsor
summary: A distributed storage cluster that serves S3 buckets, block devices and a file system from the same pool of disks.
intro: Ceph is built on RADOS, a cluster of storage daemons that keeps everything as objects in a flat namespace. Each disk runs an OSD daemon, and a small group of monitors keeps the cluster map and agrees on changes to it with Paxos. Clients don’t ask a central server where data lives: they hash an object’s name into a placement group and run CRUSH, a placement function, to map that group onto OSDs according to rules such as “one copy per host” or “one per rack”. Each pool is either replicated (three copies is typical) or erasure-coded, and the OSDs copy, check and repair data among themselves when a disk fails.

Three gateways sit on top. The RADOS Gateway (`radosgw`, or RGW) is an HTTP server that speaks a large subset of the S3 API, plus OpenStack Swift: it keeps each bucket’s index as key-value data (omap) on RADOS objects in an index pool and stores object contents in a data pool. RBD serves block devices to VMs and Kubernetes volumes, and CephFS adds a POSIX file system with its own metadata servers. New clusters are usually deployed with `cephadm`, which runs every daemon in a container. On Kubernetes, Rook, a CNCF graduated operator, runs Ceph for you: you declare a `CephCluster` and a `CephObjectStore`, Rook creates the pools and RGW pods, and apps can request buckets with an `ObjectBucketClaim`.
strengths: One cluster serves S3 buckets, block volumes and a shared file system, so a single platform and team can cover all three
Broad S3 coverage: versioning, Object Lock, bucket policies, lifecycle rules, server-side encryption and notifications to Kafka, AMQP or HTTP, plus the Swift API
CRUSH rules spread copies across hosts, racks or rooms, and the cluster recovers by itself when disks or nodes fail
Multisite RGW replicates between zones in different data centres, and every zone can accept writes
Mature and widely deployed: research since 2004, a foundation-backed community and commercial support from IBM and others
limits: Far more to run than a single S3 server: monitors, managers, OSDs and gateways, each with its own failure modes and upgrade steps
Hungry for hardware: monitors need a majority to agree, so plan for at least three hosts, and each OSD targets 4 GB of RAM by default (about 48 GB for a 12-disk node)
Performance depends on tuning: the docs say the bucket index and data pools need placement-group tuning beyond the defaults, and a wrong CRUSH rule can put copies in the same failure domain
S3 support is a large subset, not all of it: bucket replication works only between RGW zones, and some headers and canned ACLs differ from AWS

sections.title: Moving from MinIO
body: RGW covers nearly everything MinIO users rely on: versioning, Object Lock, bucket policies, lifecycle rules, server-side encryption, notifications and cross-site replication. The difference is the platform underneath. MinIO is one binary per server; Ceph is a cluster with its own operating model, so budget time to learn `ceph` and `radosgw-admin`, or let Rook run it if you are already on Kubernetes. Pick Ceph when you also want block or file storage, or need to grow to many petabytes; for buckets alone, a lighter store is less work.

Data moves over the S3 API. Create users with `radosgw-admin`, recreate buckets and their policies, then copy objects with `rclone sync minio:bucket ceph:bucket` (rclone has a `Ceph` provider setting). Run the sync again just before cutover to catch new writes, then switch the endpoint in your apps. Users, policies, lifecycle rules and notification targets don’t travel with the objects and have to be recreated, and a plain sync copies only current versions, not older ones.

story: Ceph began as Sage Weil’s PhD research at the University of California, Santa Cruz, funded by Lawrence Livermore, Sandia and Los Alamos national laboratories, which needed storage that could scale across thousands of disks. Weil wrote the first code in 2004. In November 2006 he presented the Ceph file system at OSDI and CRUSH, its placement algorithm, at SC ’06. RADOS, the object store underneath, followed in 2007, the year he finished his thesis.

Weil kept working on Ceph full-time after graduating, and in 2010 its client was merged into the Linux kernel. In 2012 he founded Inktank to sell support. Red Hat bought Inktank in 2014 for about $175 million; Inktank’s customers already included CERN and Cisco, and many early OpenStack clouds ran on Ceph’s object and block storage.

The Linux Foundation launched the Ceph Foundation in 2018. At the start of 2023 Red Hat’s Ceph team moved to IBM, which became the foundation’s premier sponsor and said its Ceph products would stay 100% open source and upstream-first.

choices.choice: Compute where data lives instead of looking it up
choices.why: A central table of every object’s location becomes a bottleneck at petabyte scale. With CRUSH, every client and OSD calculates locations from a small cluster map and talks to the right disks directly.
OSDs replicate data, watch their peers and recover lost copies themselves, so the monitors stay small and the cluster heals without a central coordinator.
Building block devices, a file system and an S3 gateway on the same RADOS layer means one cluster can serve VMs, shared directories and buckets.
